Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(InStyle.com) -- Style-maker, TV host and opinionated fashionista Carson Kressley explains how to give yourself a complete makeover--inside and out. Style-maker Carson Kressley spills the naked truth on giving yourself a mental makeover. Minimize the negative . As Coco Chanel said, "Fashion is architecture: It's a matter of proportions." In other words: No matter which part of your body you dislike, there's a clever way to divert the eye elsewhere. Try different styles and employ horizontal (widening), vertical (elongating) and diagonal (slimming) lines as necessary. Venture out of your comfort zone . "Many women get used to dressing their body a certain way because they think it's the only thing that works for them," says Kressley. Find a boutique or department store with well-trained salespeople and try on three styles you've never worn. It might be a fabric such as jersey that you've always deemed too clingy or an Empire-waist camisole that you're convinced looks too young. Not every experiment will be a success, but even one new style or color will prove that there are more ways than you thought to look your best. Don't be ruled by your insecurities . If you've been avoiding the beach or missing out on parties because you're afraid of being the largest person there, grab a friend and go to the very place that incites terror--just be sure you're wearing an amazing outfit. Avoid a blackout . "Have you ever seen a happy goth?" muses Kressley. "I think everyone needs color to feel good." Too many women rely on head-to-toe black as a form of camouflage. But any hue can be slimming if worn monochromatically--so instead of black, reach for plum, gray or chocolate brown. Clean out your closet . Whether you're holding on to clothes that are too small because you hope you'll fit into them someday, or clothes that are too big for fear you'll grow back into them, you're keeping past wounds open. "Old clothes stop you from living in the present," says Kressley. "They reinforce what you used to look like." Get rid of anything you haven't worn in two years and replace it with something new that makes you feel pretty. And while you're out shopping, have a house-cleaner swing by for good measure. Write yourself a love note . Some women are so obsessed with their hips that they fail to notice their flat tummy. Remind yourself of your virtues by writing a note that says something like "Hey, you have a great chest!" Tack it to the bathroom mirror so you'll see it in the morning and before bedtime. "We're so trained to look for the negative that we need a physical reminder of the positive," explains Kressley. Have a princess moment . Treating yourself to a massage, a body exfoliation, a professional blow-out, a brow shaping or a mani-pedi can elevate your mood by affirming to yourself that you're worth the splurge. Get naked . Some women on Kressley's show are so self-conscious about their bodies that they're reluctant to be naked around their husbands. That discomfort affects how they feel when dressed too. Before you can move as if you own the room, you'll have to be at ease inside your skin, and spending time in the buff can help. One idea: Take a bath with the (gasp!) lights on--no candles. "Feeling comfortable with your body alone is the first step to feeling comfortable with your body around others," says Kressley. If all else fails, fake it . One of Kressley's favorite mantras is "looking cute is feeling cute." So if you're having a low day, force yourself to go through the motions. Put on your makeup, do your hair, wear a great outfit. Sometimes faking it can give you enough of a boost to lift you out of the doldrums. "Feeling pretty," Kressley says, "changes your whole outlook because you feel good about yourself." outputs.L1:
**(InStyle.com) —** Style-maker, TV host, and outspoken fashionista Carson Kressley explains how to give yourself a complete makeover—inside and out—and spills the naked truth about achieving a mental makeover.

### Minimize the Negative

As Coco Chanel said, “Fashion is architecture: It’s a matter of proportions.” In other words, no matter which part of your body you dislike, there is a clever way to draw the eye elsewhere. Experiment with different styles, using horizontal lines to widen, vertical lines to elongate, and diagonal lines to slim, as needed.

### Venture Outside Your Comfort Zone

“Many women get used to dressing their body a certain way because they think it’s the only thing that works for them,” says Kressley.

Visit a boutique or department store with well-trained salespeople and try on three styles you have never worn before. It might be a fabric such as jersey, which you have always considered too clingy, or an Empire-waist camisole that you are convinced looks too young. Not every experiment will succeed, but discovering even one new style or color will prove that there are more ways to look your best than you may have thought.

### Don’t Be Ruled by Your Insecurities

If you have been avoiding the beach or missing parties because you are afraid of being the largest person there, grab a friend and go to the very place that inspires such fear—just make sure you are wearing an amazing outfit.

### Avoid a Blackout

“Have you ever seen a happy goth?” Kressley muses. “I think everyone needs color to feel good.”

Too many women rely on head-to-toe black as a form of camouflage. But any color can be slimming when worn monochromatically, so instead of black, reach for plum, gray, or chocolate brown.

### Clean Out Your Closet

Whether you are holding on to clothes that are too small because you hope to fit into them someday, or clothes that are too large because you fear growing back into them, you are keeping old wounds open.

“Old clothes stop you from living in the present,” says Kressley. “They reinforce what you used to look like.”

Get rid of anything you have not worn in two years and replace it with something new that makes you feel pretty. While you are out shopping, have a house cleaner stop by for good measure.

### Write Yourself a Love Note

Some women become so preoccupied with their hips that they fail to notice their flat stomach. Remind yourself of your best features by writing a note that says something like, “Hey, you have a great chest!” Post it on the bathroom mirror so you will see it in the morning and again before bed.

“We’re so trained to look for the negative that we need a physical reminder of the positive,” Kressley explains.

### Have a Princess Moment

Treating yourself to a massage, body exfoliation, professional blowout, brow shaping, or mani-pedi can elevate your mood by affirming that you are worth the splurge.

### Get Naked

Some women on Kressley’s show are so self-conscious about their bodies that they are reluctant to be naked around their husbands. That discomfort also affects how they feel when dressed. Before you can move as though you own the room, you must feel at ease in your own skin—and spending time in the buff can help.

One idea: Take a bath with the—gasp!—lights on and no candles.

“Feeling comfortable with your body alone is the first step to feeling comfortable with your body around others,” says Kressley.

### If All Else Fails, Fake It

One of Kressley’s favorite mantras is, “Looking cute is feeling cute.” If you are having a low day, force yourself to go through the motions: Put on your makeup, style your hair, and wear a great outfit. Sometimes, faking it can provide enough of a boost to lift you out of the doldrums.

“Feeling pretty,” Kressley says, “changes your whole outlook because you feel good about yourself.”

outputs.L2:
**(InStyle.com)** — Television host, style expert and outspoken fashion personality Carson Kressley shares advice for transforming both your appearance and your state of mind. Here are his candid tips for building confidence from the inside out.

### Shift attention away from what bothers you  
Coco Chanel famously described fashion as architecture governed by proportion. That means any area of your body you feel unhappy with can be balanced by directing attention somewhere else. Experiment with silhouettes and use horizontal lines to create width, vertical lines to add length and diagonal lines to produce a slimmer effect.

### Try something unfamiliar  
Kressley says many women repeatedly dress the same way because they believe it is the only approach that flatters their shape. Visit a boutique or department store where the staff is knowledgeable, and test three looks you have never worn before. You might try jersey, even if you have always considered it too clingy, or an Empire-waist camisole you assumed was too youthful. Some choices may not work, but discovering even one flattering color or style can show you that you have more options than you realized.

### Refuse to let insecurity make your decisions  
If fear of being the biggest person in the room has kept you away from beaches or parties, ask a friend to accompany you and face the situation that frightens you. Just make sure you go in an outfit that makes you look and feel fantastic.

### Don’t hide entirely in black  
Kressley jokingly asks whether anyone has ever encountered a cheerful goth, adding that he believes color helps people feel better. Many women use all-black outfits as camouflage, but black is not the only slimming choice. Wearing any single color from head to toe can create the same effect, so consider plum, gray or chocolate brown instead.

### Clear out outdated clothing  
Keeping garments that are too small because you hope to wear them again—or oversized pieces because you worry you may need them later—allows old emotional pain to linger. According to Kressley, clothes from the past prevent you from fully inhabiting the present because they keep reminding you of how you once looked. Discard anything you have not worn for two years, then replace it with something new that makes you feel attractive. While you are shopping, you might even arrange for a cleaner to refresh your home.

### Leave yourself an encouraging message  
A woman may focus so intensely on her hips that she overlooks her flat stomach. Make your positive qualities harder to ignore by writing yourself a compliment, such as a reminder that you have a wonderful chest. Place the note on your bathroom mirror, where you will see it in the morning and again before going to bed. Kressley explains that because people are conditioned to notice flaws, they sometimes need a visible prompt to recognize their strengths.

### Give yourself royal treatment  
A massage, body scrub, salon blowout, eyebrow shaping, manicure or pedicure can improve your spirits. Spending money on personal care also reinforces the idea that you deserve to be pampered.

### Become comfortable without clothes  
Some women featured on Kressley’s program feel so uneasy about their bodies that they hesitate to undress in front of their husbands. That self-consciousness also influences how they feel while clothed. To carry yourself with complete confidence, you first need to feel at home in your own body, and occasionally being nude may help. One suggestion is to take a bath with the regular lights on rather than relying on candles. Kressley says that accepting your body in private is the beginning of feeling comfortable with it around other people.

### When necessary, act confident until you feel it  
One of Kressley’s preferred sayings links looking adorable with feeling adorable. On a difficult day, go through your usual beauty routine even if you do not feel motivated: apply makeup, style your hair and choose an excellent outfit. Performing those actions can sometimes provide enough emotional momentum to pull you out of a slump. Kressley says that feeling attractive can transform your perspective because it improves the way you feel about yourself.

outputs.L3:
Dressing with confidence begins by understanding how proportions, cuts, and clothing lines can shape the overall appearance of an outfit. Strategic choices can draw attention away from areas you feel less comfortable with while highlighting the features you appreciate most. The goal is not to hide your body, but to create balance and wear clothes that help you feel comfortable and self-assured.

It is also helpful to step outside your comfort zone. Try unfamiliar silhouettes, fabrics, patterns, and colors rather than automatically choosing the same styles. Knowledgeable salespeople or stylists can suggest options you may not have considered and help you find flattering combinations. Even if every experiment is not successful, exploring new possibilities can gradually expand your sense of personal style.

Most importantly, do not allow body insecurities to keep you from attending social events or enjoying meaningful experiences. You do not need to reach a particular size or look a certain way before participating fully in life. Choose an outfit that makes you feel at ease, focus on the people and activities around you, and remember that confidence often grows through participation rather than avoidance.

If you tend to rely on head-to-toe black, consider experimenting with monochromatic outfits in other rich, versatile shades. Plum, charcoal gray, navy, olive, or chocolate brown can create the same streamlined effect while adding warmth, depth, and variety to your wardrobe. Different textures and subtle tonal variations can make a single-color outfit feel polished and visually interesting.

Finally, clear out clothes that no longer fit or suit your current lifestyle. Holding on to them—especially as reminders of a former size—can keep you focused on the past instead of appreciating yourself in the present. Keep clothing that fits comfortably, reflects who you are now, and supports the life you currently lead. A wardrobe filled with wearable, confidence-building pieces makes getting dressed easier and more enjoyable.
outputs.L4:
Carson Kressley believes a successful makeover begins on the inside and works its way out. Clothing can help people recognize their strengths, challenge old insecurities, and present themselves with greater confidence. Rather than focusing on size or trying to hide every perceived flaw, he recommends choosing silhouettes that create flattering proportions and highlight the features a person already likes. The goal is not to follow rigid rules, but to discover what feels balanced, comfortable, and authentic.

That process often requires trying unfamiliar styles. People may automatically reject certain colors, cuts, or trends because they assume those options will not suit them. Kressley encourages experimentation before judgment: try the garment on, look at the full outfit, and notice how it changes posture and attitude. A supportive fitting, a new hairstyle, or another confidence-building experience can help someone see possibilities that insecurity had previously obscured.

Color is another useful tool. A monochromatic outfit does not have to mean dressing entirely in black or neutral shades. Wearing related tones of a bright, flattering color can create a long, cohesive line while still looking lively and modern. Variations in texture, fabric, and shade add interest without breaking the streamlined effect. Accessories can then provide contrast or personality.

A makeover also involves letting go. Closets often contain clothes that no longer fit, reflect an earlier stage of life, or carry unrealistic expectations about the future. Keeping such items can create guilt and make getting dressed more difficult. Kressley advises removing outdated, unflattering, or unused pieces so that the remaining wardrobe supports the person as they are now.

Ultimately, style improves when people become willing to move beyond familiar fears. Experimenting with proportion, color, and unexpected silhouettes can reveal many more ways to look good than they previously imagined. At the same time, clearing away clothes tied to the past makes room for a wardrobe—and a life—grounded in the present. The result is more than a new appearance: it is a stronger sense of confidence, possibility, and self-acceptance.

Carson’s approach to fashion is a perfect match for the modern **InStyle** reader: confident, polished, and effortlessly personal. Rather than following every trend, Carson focuses on timeless pieces, expressive accessories, and combinations that feel both fresh and wearable.

What makes Carson’s **style** stand out is the balance between classic and contemporary. A tailored blazer might be paired with relaxed denim, while bold colors or statement shoes add individuality. Each look proves that great fashion is not simply about what you wear—it is about how you make it your own.

In true **InStyle** fashion, Carson shows that confidence is the best accessory. Whether dressing for a special event or creating an elevated everyday outfit, the key is choosing clothes that feel authentic, comfortable, and memorable.
